question: Who is required by Texas law to complete an approved boater education course and carry a Boater Education Certificate?
choice_a: Anyone born on or after September 1, 1993 who operates a motorboat with more than 15 horsepower, a PWC, or a windblown vessel over 14 feet
choice_b: Everyone who operates any vessel in Texas, regardless of birth date
choice_c: Only people who operate vessels for commercial purposes
choice_d: No one; Texas has never had a boater education requirement
explanation: Texas mandates boater education for anyone born on or after September 1, 1993 who operates a motorboat over 15 horsepower, a PWC, or a windblown vessel more than 14 feet long.

question: Is there a single official TPWD-administered boating exam that every Texas boater must take at a state office?
choice_a: Yes, every boater must appear in person at a TPWD office to take a standardized state exam
choice_b: No -- TPWD approves NASBLA-standard third-party course providers (such as Boat-Ed, BOATERexam, and BOATsmart!), and the course's own final exam serves as the certification test
choice_c: Yes, but only for PWC operators, not other motorboat operators
choice_d: No exam of any kind is required to obtain a Texas Boater Education Certificate
explanation: Like most states, Texas does not run its own single boating exam. TPWD approves NASBLA-standard course providers, and completing that provider's course (culminating in its own final exam) satisfies the mandatory education requirement and results in a Boater Education Certificate.
source_note: TPWD Boater Education program structure -- approved provider model

question: How long is a Texas Boater Education Certificate valid?
choice_a: It must be renewed every year
choice_c: It is valid for life and never needs to be renewed
choice_d: It expires as soon as the holder turns 18
explanation: A Texas Boater Education Certificate, once earned, is valid for the boater's lifetime and does not require periodic renewal.
source_note: TPWD Mandatory Boater Education Requirements -- certificate validity

question: What must a person subject to the mandatory boater education law have in their possession while operating a boat in Texas?
choice_a: Nothing; no documentation is ever required to be carried aboard
choice_b: Only their vehicle driver's license, with no boating-specific document
choice_c: A separate license plate for the vessel itself
choice_d: A picture identification card and their Boater Education Certificate (or card)
explanation: Persons subject to the mandatory boater education requirement must carry photo identification along with their Boater Education Certificate while operating a covered vessel.
source_note: TPWD Mandatory Boater Education Requirements -- proof of completion

question: Does completing a boater education course from another state satisfy the Texas requirement?
choice_a: Yes, as long as the other state's course was NASBLA-approved
choice_b: No, only a Texas-issued certificate is ever accepted
choice_c: Only if the other state is Louisiana or Oklahoma
choice_d: Out-of-state certificates are accepted only for PWC operators
explanation: Texas accepts boater education certificates from other states as long as those courses were approved by NASBLA (National Association of State Boating Law Administrators), reflecting the nationwide reciprocity built into the NASBLA standard.
source_note: TPWD Mandatory Boater Education Requirements -- reciprocity

question: Which vessels must be titled in Texas, regardless of length?
choice_b: All motorized vessels, including any sailboat with an auxiliary engine
choice_c: No vessel is required to be titled in Texas under any circumstance
explanation: Texas requires all motorized vessels to be titled regardless of length, including sailboats equipped with an auxiliary motor, along with non-motorized vessels 14 feet and longer.
source_note: TPWD Title, Registration, Tax & ID Requirements

question: Which small vessels are exempt from Texas titling and registration requirements?
choice_a: All vessels under 26 feet, motorized or not
choice_b: All PWCs, since they are considered recreational toys rather than vessels
choice_c: Non-motorized canoes, kayaks, rowboats, and similar vessels under 14 feet that are paddled, poled, oared, or windblown, as long as no motor is added
choice_d: No vessel is exempt from titling or registration in Texas
explanation: Small non-motorized paddle craft under 14 feet are exempt from Texas titling and registration; adding an outboard or trolling motor removes the exemption.
source_note: TPWD Title, Registration, Tax & ID Requirements -- exemptions

question: What titling exemption exists for certain older, low-horsepower outboard motors in Texas?
choice_a: No outboard motor of any age or horsepower is ever exempt from titling
choice_b: All outboard motors over 10 horsepower are exempt
choice_c: Only motors manufactured in Texas are exempt
choice_d: Internal combustion outboard motors 40 years or older and 25 horsepower or less are exempt from titling, as are all electric outboard motors
explanation: Texas exempts internal combustion outboard motors that are at least 40 years old and 25 horsepower or less, as well as all-electric outboard motors, from the titling requirement.
source_note: TPWD Title, Registration, Tax & ID Requirements -- outboard motor exemptions

question: What authority do Texas game wardens have when it comes to enforcing boating laws on public water?
choice_a: They may stop, board, and inspect vessels for safety equipment and registration compliance, and enforce laws including BWI, reckless operation, and fishing/hunting regulations
choice_b: Game wardens have no authority over recreational boaters, only over hunters
choice_c: Only local police, never game wardens, may enforce boating laws in Texas
choice_d: Game wardens may only issue warnings, never citations or arrests
explanation: Texas game wardens are fully commissioned peace officers with broad authority to stop, board, and inspect vessels, and to enforce boating safety laws including BWI and reckless operation, in addition to fish and wildlife regulations.
source_note: TPWD game warden law enforcement authority

question: What deferral option exists for someone who needs to operate a covered vessel before completing the mandatory boater education course?
choice_a: No deferral of any kind exists; the course must be completed before ever operating the vessel
choice_b: A temporary deferral (for a limited period, for a fee) is available to allow operation while the person completes the required course
choice_c: Deferrals are unlimited and never expire
choice_d: A deferral is available only to out-of-state visitors
explanation: Texas offers a short-term deferral option, for a modest fee, giving a person temporary relief from the boater education requirement while they complete an approved course.
source_note: TPWD Mandatory Boater Education Requirements -- deferral option

question: How does completing a U.S. Coast Guard vessel operator's license affect the Texas boater education requirement?
choice_a: A USCG license has no bearing on the Texas boater education requirement
choice_b: A USCG license satisfies the requirement only for operating PWCs, not other motorboats
choice_c: Proof of completing the requirements for a USCG-issued vessel operator's license satisfies the Texas boater education requirement
choice_d: A USCG license only counts if it was issued in Texas
explanation: Texas recognizes proof of completing the requirements for a USCG-issued vessel operator's license as satisfying its mandatory boater education requirement.
source_note: TPWD Mandatory Boater Education Requirements -- USCG license exemption

question: What free option does TPWD offer for paddlers (canoe, kayak, and paddleboard users) who are not otherwise subject to mandatory boater education?
choice_a: TPWD offers no safety resources at all for non-motorized paddle craft
choice_b: Paddlers are required to complete the same paid course as motorboat operators
choice_c: A mandatory in-person paddling exam administered only in Austin
choice_d: A free online paddling safety course, though it does not itself satisfy the mandatory boater education requirement for motorized vessels
explanation: TPWD offers a free online safety course tailored to canoe, kayak, and paddleboard users, though this voluntary course does not substitute for the mandatory boater education certificate required for motorized vessel operation.
source_note: TPWD Mandatory Boater Education Requirements -- paddler resources

question: Where must a vessel's Texas registration numbers and validation decals be displayed?
choice_a: The registration number must be painted or attached to both sides of the forward half of the vessel and be clearly legible, with the current decal displayed as required
choice_b: Registration numbers may be displayed anywhere on the vessel, including underwater surfaces
choice_c: Texas vessels are not required to display any registration numbers
choice_d: Registration numbers only need to be displayed on the trailer, not the vessel itself
explanation: Texas requires registration numbers to be permanently affixed to both sides of the forward half of the vessel in a clear, legible, contrasting color, along with the current validation decal.
source_note: TPWD Title, Registration, Tax & ID Requirements -- display of registration numbers
